title: IBM, AMD, And Oak Ridge Unveil Quantum Error Correction Platform
gist: IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge's Quantum Science Center unveiled a co-located quantum-classical co-design platform in Poughkeepsie pairing IBM's 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 with ORNL's AMD Turin/MI355X-based Umbra system for error-correction, decoding and AI workflow research. IBM says the DOE Quantum Genesis Mission target of 100 logical qubits running 100,000 operations by late 2028 requires a 238-fold jump from its July 70-logical-qubit demo, and ties the work to its 2029 fault-tolerant Starling system.

themes.theme: Error correction is the gating problem

insights.claim: Quantum systems today typically have gate error rates of one per 100 to 1,000 operations, which must improve significantly before fault-tolerant quantum computing is possible.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Error rates, not qubit counts, are the KPI to track for commercial quantum timelines.
insights.quote: Quantum systems typically now have gate error rates ranging from one error per 100 to 1,000 operations.
insights.locator: Each effort is made to reach

insights.claim: IBM research claims hierarchical error correction, layering an inner module-level code with an outer code, could reach a trillion logical operations at a physical error rate of one in 1,000 while keeping hardware and connectivity demands simpler.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: If true, fault tolerance may be reachable without dramatic physical qubit improvements, lowering scaling cost.
insights.quote: the approach could reach a trillion logical operations at a physical qubit error rate of one in 1,000

insights.claim: IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge's Quantum Science Center built a co-design platform that places quantum computers and classical HPC in the same location, which IBM says rarely happens because most pairings connect via cloud APIs, adding complexity and latency.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Low-latency colocation becomes a differentiator, favoring vendors who can bundle QPUs with HPC.

insights.claim: The platform, housed at IBM's Poughkeepsie facility, combines IBM's 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 chip with Oak Ridge's Umbra HPC system powered by AMD fifth-gen Epyc Turin 9005 CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPUs for error correction, decoding optimization and orchestration.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: AMD gains a foothold as the classical compute partner in quantum-centric supercomputing.

insights.claim: QPUs are expected to act as another accelerator alongside GPUs and TPUs in hybrid supercomputers, with AI serving as the connective tissue between quantum and classical systems.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Quantum adds to rather than displaces GPU demand; hybrid systems expand the HPC TAM.

insights.claim: GPUs on the platform will run AI models used to develop better quantum algorithms, workflows and error-correction methods, and will test latency-sensitive classical decoding.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Quantum error correction creates incremental classical GPU workload.
insights.quote: “The GPUs that are part of the co-design platform will play a key role in running the AI models or algorithms that scientists plan to develop and improve upon.”

insights.claim: IBM's Nighthawk moves from the heavy-hex architecture to a square lattice where most qubits connect to four neighbors, about 60% more connectivity, enabling shorter execution times and compatibility with standard surface code.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: A notable IBM architecture pivot toward mainstream surface-code error correction.
insights.quote: about a 60 percent increase in connectivity over heavy-hex

insights.claim: IBM's quantum API exposes deep pulse control, letting researchers measure qubits mid-calculation and act on results in real time, including timing signals to protect qubits from noise.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Low-level control access is a software moat for platform stickiness among researchers.

insights.claim: IBM and the University of Chicago demonstrated experiments with up to 70 logical qubits and 438 hard operations in July 2026.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Baseline for measuring progress toward government fault-tolerance targets.

insights.claim: The DOE Quantum Genesis Mission's Q Competition targets 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028, requiring a 238-fold increase in hard operation count, which IBM calls feasible but demanding fast progress.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: Defines a concrete 2028 milestone that will reveal which quantum vendors are on track.
insights.quote: “To reach this goal, the broader quantum community needs to achieve a 238-fold increase in hard operation count, and we need to do it fast.

insights.claim: IBM plans to deliver its fault-tolerant Quantum Starling system by 2029 and will use the co-design platform's work in developing it.
insights.speaker: Jeff Burt
insights.so_what: 2029 Starling is IBM's key dated fault-tolerance commitment for investors to track.
